paragraphs: “It must be a sign from heaven,” others rushed to add, and nobody objected; that view was taken up at once. People also pointed out that natural decay, as in any dead sinner, would have shown later, after twenty-four hours at least. This early rotting “was in excess of nature,” so the finger of God was plain. It was a sign. The argument seemed beyond answering.

Gentle Father Iosif, the librarian, one of the dead man’s great favorites, tried to answer some of the spiteful talkers. “This is not held everywhere alike,” he told them. Bodies of the just staying free of decay was no dogma of the Orthodox Church, he said, merely an opinion. Even in the most Orthodox lands, on Athos for instance, the smell of decay did not greatly disturb people. There the chief mark of a saved soul’s glorification was not an incorrupt body but the color of the bones, once the body had lain in the earth for many years and rotted away. “And if the bones are yellow as wax, that is the great sign that the Lord has glorified the dead saint. If they are black instead of yellow, it shows God did not think him worthy of such glory. That is what they believe on Athos, a great place, where Orthodox doctrine has been kept from ancient times, unbroken and in its purest form,” Father Iosif concluded.

But the meek Father’s words did little good and even brought a sneering answer. “That’s all pedantry and innovation, no point listening to it,” the monks decided. “We hold to the old teaching. Nowadays there are innovations of every kind. Do we have to follow them all?” others said.

“We’ve had as many holy fathers as they have. Look at them there among the Turks, they’ve forgotten everything. Their doctrine has been unclean for ages, and they haven’t even got bells,” the most sneering of them put in.

Father Iosif walked away, grieved all the more because he had put his opinion forward so timidly, as if he hardly believed it himself. He could see, to his distress, that something very unseemly was beginning, and that disobedience was plainly on its way. One by one, all the sensible monks were silenced, as Father Iosif had been. The result was that everyone who loved the elder and had accepted the eldership with devout obedience was suddenly crushed, and exchanged timid glances when they met. The enemies of elders, who saw the institution as a novelty, now carried their heads proudly. “The late elder Varsonofy gave off no smell of corruption, but a sweet fragrance,” they reminded everyone, with spite. “But he earned that glory not as an elder, but as a holy man.”

After that came a flood of criticism and even blame for Father Zossima. “His teaching was false. He taught that life is a great joy, not a vale of tears,” said some of the less reasonable. “He went along with the fashionable belief. He didn’t admit that hell has real fire,” others, still less reasonable, added. “He wasn’t strict about fasting. He treated himself to sweets, ate cherry jam with his tea. Ladies sent it to him. Is it right for a monk under strict rule to drink tea?” some of the envious were heard to say. “He sat in pride,” the most spiteful said vengefully. “He thought himself a saint, and took it as his due when people knelt to him.” “He abused the sacrament of confession,” the fiercest enemies of the eldership added in a malicious whisper. Some of the oldest monks were among them, the strictest in their devotion, true ascetics, who had held their tongues while the elder lived and now suddenly let them loose. This was terrible, because their words weighed heavily with the young monks, whose convictions were not yet firm. The monk from Obdorsk listened closely to all this, sighing deeply and nodding. “Yes, Father Ferapont was plainly right in what he said yesterday.” And at that very moment Father Ferapont himself arrived, as if on purpose to make the confusion worse.

I have already said that he rarely left his wooden cell by the apiary. He was hardly ever seen at church either. They excused this because he was crazy, and did not hold him to the rules that applied to everyone else. To tell the whole truth, though, they had little choice. It would have looked bad to press the common rules on such a great ascetic, who prayed day and night (he even dropped off to sleep on his knees). Had they insisted, the monks would have said, “He is holier than any of us, and his rule is harder than ours. If he stays away from church, it’s because he knows when he should go. He has a rule of his own.” To avoid sinful grumbling like this, Father Ferapont was left alone.

Everyone knew that Father Ferapont had a particular dislike of Father Zossima. Now word had reached him in his hut that “God’s judgment is not the same as man’s,” and that something had happened that was “in excess of nature.” We can fairly assume that one of the first to run to him with this news was the monk from Obdorsk, who had visited him the evening before and left his cell terror-stricken.

I have said above that Father Païssy stood firm and unmoving over the coffin, reading the Gospel, and could neither hear nor see what went on outside the cell. Still, he read most of it rightly in his heart, since he knew the men around him well. It did not shake him. He waited without fear for what would come next, watching shrewdly and keenly to see how the general excitement would end.

Suddenly a tremendous uproar in the passage, in open disregard of decorum, reached his ears. The door was thrown open, and Father Ferapont stood in the doorway. A crowd of monks could be seen behind him, with many townspeople. They did not enter the cell, though. They stayed at the foot of the steps, waiting to see what Father Ferapont would say or do. Bold as they were, they felt a certain awe and knew he had not come for nothing. Standing in the doorway, Father Ferapont raised his arms, and under his right arm the sharp, prying little eyes of the monk from Obdorsk peered in. He alone, so intensely curious, could not help running up the steps after Father Ferapont. The rest, by contrast, drew back in sudden alarm when the door crashed open. With his hands held high, Father Ferapont suddenly roared:

“Casting out I cast out!” And turning every which way, he began at once to make the sign of the cross toward each of the cell’s four walls and four corners, one after another. All who had come with Father Ferapont knew at once what he was doing. They knew he did this wherever he went, and that he would neither sit down nor say a word until he had driven out the evil spirits.
“Satan, get out! Satan, get out!” he said at each sign of the cross. “Casting out I cast out,” he roared again.

He wore his coarse gown belted with a rope. Under his hempen shirt his bare chest could be seen, covered with gray hair. His feet were bare. The moment he began waving his arms, the cruel irons he wore under his gown could be heard clanking.
Father Païssy broke off his reading, stepped forward and stood in front of him, waiting.
“Why have you come, worthy Father? Why do you break good order? Why do you trouble the peace of the flock?” he said at last, with a stern look.

“Why have I come? You ask me why? What is your faith?” Father Ferapont shouted, like a madman. “I’ve come to drive out your guests, the unclean devils. I’ve come to see how many have crowded in while I was away. I want to sweep them out with a birch broom.”
“You drive out the evil spirit, but maybe you serve him yourself,” Father Païssy went on, unafraid. “And who can say of himself, ‘I am holy’? Can you, Father?”

“I’m unclean, not holy. I wouldn’t sit in an armchair, and I wouldn’t let them bow down to me like an idol,” Father Ferapont thundered. “These days folk are destroying the true faith. The dead man, your saint,” and he turned to the crowd and pointed at the coffin, “didn’t believe in devils. He gave out medicine against the devils. So now they’re as thick as spiders in the corners. And now he himself has started to stink. In that we see a great sign from God.”

What he meant was this. One of the monks was tormented by visions of evil spirits, in his dreams and later even awake. In deadly terror he told Father Zossima, and the elder told him to pray without ceasing and fast strictly. When that did no good, the elder told him to take a certain medicine as well, while going on with prayer and fasting. Many were shocked at the time and shook their heads over it, and Father Ferapont most of all, since some of the fault-finders had rushed to report to him this “extraordinary” advice from the elder.

“Go away, Father!” Father Païssy said, in a voice of command. “Judging is for God, not for man. Perhaps what we see here is a ‘sign’ that you cannot understand, nor I, nor any of us. Go, Father, and do not disturb the flock!” he repeated with emphasis.

“He didn’t keep the fasts by the rule, and that’s why the sign has come. That’s plain, and it’s a sin to hide it,” the fanatic answered, swept along by a zeal that ran ahead of his reason, and he would not be quiet. “Sweetmeats led him astray. Ladies brought them to him in their pockets. He sipped tea, he worshiped his belly, stuffing it with sweet things and his mind with proud thoughts.... And for this he’s put to shame....”

“You are speaking rashly, Father.” Father Païssy, too, raised his voice. “I admire your fasting and your hardships, but you talk rashly, like some frivolous boy, fickle and childish. Go away, Father. I command you!” Father Païssy thundered, finishing.

“I’m going,” said Ferapont, looking a little thrown, but just as bitter. “You learned men! You’re so clever you look down on my lowliness. I came here with little learning, and what I did know I’ve forgotten here. God Himself has protected me in my weakness from your cleverness.”

Father Païssy stood over him, resolute, waiting. Father Ferapont fell silent. Then, suddenly resting his cheek on his hand in dejection, he said in a sing-song voice, with his eyes on the dead elder’s coffin:

“Tomorrow they’ll sing ‘Our Helper and Defender’ over him—a splendid anthem—and over me, when I die, they’ll sing only ‘What earthly joy’—a little canticle,”[6] he added with tearful regret. “You’re proud and puffed up. This place is vanity!” he suddenly shouted like a madman, and with a wave of his hand he turned sharply and hurried down the steps. The crowd waiting below wavered. Some followed him at once, some hung back, since the cell was still open, and Father Païssy came out onto the steps after Father Ferapont and stood watching him. But the worked-up old fanatic was not entirely silenced. Twenty steps off, he suddenly turned toward the setting sun, threw up both arms and, as if someone had cut him down, dropped to the ground with a loud scream.

“My God has conquered! Christ has conquered the setting sun!” he shouted wildly, stretching his hands up toward the sun. Then he fell on his face and sobbed like a small child, his body shaking with tears, his arms spread out on the ground. At that they all rushed up to him. There were cries and sobs of sympathy ... a sort of frenzy seemed to seize them all.
“This is the one who is a saint! This is the one who is a holy man!” some cried out, their fear gone. “This is the one who ought to be elder,” others added spitefully.

“He wouldn’t be elder ... he’d refuse ... he wouldn’t serve a cursed innovation ... he wouldn’t copy their foolery,” other voices joined in at once. It is hard to say how far they might have gone, but just then the bell rang for service. They all began to cross themselves together. Father Ferapont, too, got up and, crossing himself, went back to his cell without looking round, still crying out words that made no sense at all. A few went after him, but most scattered, hurrying to service. Father Païssy had Father Iosif read in his place and went down. The wild shouting of bigots could not shake him, but his heart was suddenly filled with sadness, for some particular reason, and he felt it. He stopped and asked himself suddenly, “Why am I sad, even to dejection?” and at once realized, to his surprise, that his sudden sadness had a very small and particular cause. In the crowd packed at the entrance to the cell, he had noticed Alyosha, and he remembered that at the sight of him he had felt a pang in his heart. “Can that boy mean so much to my heart now?” he asked himself, wondering.

Just then Alyosha went past him, hurrying off, though not toward the church. Their eyes met. Alyosha looked away quickly and lowered his eyes to the ground, and from the boy’s look alone Father Païssy guessed what a great change was taking place in him at that moment.
“Have you, too, been led into temptation?” cried Father Païssy. “Are you with those of little faith?” he added sadly.

Alyosha stopped and looked blankly at Father Païssy, then quickly looked away again and again stared at the ground. He stood turned aside and kept his face from Father Païssy, who watched him closely.
“Where are you rushing off to? The bell is calling to service,” he asked again, but again Alyosha gave no answer.
“Are you leaving the hermitage? What, without asking leave, without asking a blessing?”

Alyosha suddenly smiled a twisted smile and gave a strange, very strange, look to the Father into whose care his former guide, the former master of his heart and mind, his beloved elder, had entrusted him as he lay dying. Then, still without a word, he waved his hand, as if he did not even care to be respectful, and walked off with quick steps toward the gates, away from the hermitage.
“You’ll come back again!” Father Païssy murmured, looking after him in sorrow and surprise.
